## Loading Datasets

First load the CRU and FAO data from Parquet Files

```{r load_fao}
#| echo: true
# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(arrow)
# Load the full fao dataset
read_parquet(
  file.path(data_path,"FAO","parquet","FAO_crop_livestock.parquet")
) |>
  filter(Item == "Avocados" & Element == "Yield") -> faostat_avocado

read_parquet(
  file.path(data_path,"CRU","parquet","tmp_w_ISO3.parquet")
) |>
  filter(Period == "ANN") -> cru_tmp_ann

faostat_avocado |>
  inner_join(cru_tmp_ann,join_by(ISO3,Year),suffix=c("_fao","_cru")) |>
  drop_na(ISO3) -> avocado_tmp
```

# What is a Model?

## Models - Framing Discussion

What is a **model**?

. . .

A simplified abstraction of reality

- Purposefully designed to approximate some system or complex phenomenon
- Intentionally simplified (why?)
- Captures first-order behavior or relationships
- Discards distracting noise or minutiae 
  

## What is the goal of a model?

Real world systems are incredibly complex

- Suppose a model ignores some biological and/or environmental realities
  - Is it still more useful than just looking at the raw historical data?
  - Why or why not?
  
## Evaluating models

What is a "good" model?

- What properties will make us prefer one model over another?
- How should we evaluate or compare potential models?
- How should we make decisions over what features to include in a model?


## Many forms of models

Models come in many forms

- Miniature analogs of physical objects (e.g., wind tunnel models)
- Simplified biological systems in controlled environments
- Sophisticated computer-based simulations
- Mathematical representations of relationships in physical, biological, or economic systems

This class will focus on the mathematical representations

## Models as math

Models can be implemented as mathematical abstractions of the real world

- Attempt to use information we know about the world
  - Called features, explanatory variables, or independent variables
- To explain some outcome we care about
  - Called labels, response variables, or dependent variables
  

## Models as math

Some symbology

- Labels are often denoted as $y$
- The collection of features denoted as $x$

We are attempting to learn about the function

$$y = f(x) + \varepsilon$$

What is $\varepsilon$ here?


## Breaking down models as math

Suppose we have the model: $y = f(x) + \varepsilon$

- $f(x)$ represents the relationship we want to uncover
- $\varepsilon$ represents the "noise"
- Why is there "noise" in this process?
- What contributes to noise?


# Goals of Modeling

## What are the goals of modeling?

In general we will have one of two objectives in building models

**Explanation**

- Determine *causal* and *structural* relationships
- Focused on relationships between specific features and the label
  - Direction/Sign
  - Magnitude
  - Statistical Precision
- Favors simple, interpretable models over predictive power
- Focus on accounting for *confounders*

## Explanation Model Examples

Examples of questions that lead to explanation models:

- Suppose average July temperatures increase by 1°C. How much do avocado yields change?
- How much can we mitigate the impacts of drought on avocado yields using advanced
fertilizers or technology?

## What are the goals of modeling?

In general we will have one of two objectives in building models

**Prediction**

- Use what we know about the world to make predictions of something we don't know
- Often using current conditions to predict the future
- Focused on *accurate* and *precise* predictions of the label
- Care about the quality of the prediction, not how individual features change predictions

## Prediction Model Examples

Examples of questions that lead to prediction models:

- Given this year's climate predictions, what do we expect avocado yields to be?
- How do we expect avocado yields to change over the next 20 years?

## Evaluating Prediction Models

How do we decide if a prediction model is "good"?

- Good predictions tend to have two attributes
- **Accuracy**: Predictions are, on average, correct
- **Precision**: Predictions have low noise or variability

Suppose I want to predict tomorrow's high temperature

- **Model 1**: I always predict it will be 75 degrees
- **Model 2**: I always predict it will be today's high temperature

# Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) Models 

## Ordinary Least Squares

We'll use [**Ordinary Least Squares**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinary_least_squares) (OLS)

- Assumes $y$ is a **linear function** of 
  - Features ($x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$) 
  - Unknown parameters ($b_0, b_1, b_2, \dots, b_n$)
- Our prediction of the label $\hat y$ is
$$\hat y = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + \dots + b_n x_n$$
- OLS finds $b$ values that minimize the Mean Square Error (MSE) of the predictions

## Mean Square Error

In OLS, we use MSE as the **loss function**

- MSE is the average of squared prediction errors 
$$MSE = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left( y_i - \hat y_i \right)^2$$
- Perfect predictions have MSE of zero
- MSE increases as predictions become less accurate
- Models with lower MSE have "better" predictions

## Loss Functions

Building a model requires choosing a **loss function**

- Allows comparing different types of prediction errors
- In general, loss functions increase as model predictions get "worse"
- Attempt to find models that minimize the loss function
- The loss function embeds **your preferences** over different types of prediction errors

## MSE Loss Function Properties

MSE averages **squared prediction errors**

|Error|Squared| |Error|Squared|
|:---:|:---:|---|:---:|:---:|
| 1 | 1 | | -1 | 1 |
| 2 | 4 | | -2 | 4 |
| 3 | 9 | | -3 | 9 |
| 4 | 16 | | -4 | 16 |

- Over- and under-predictions equally bad
- Larger errors much worse than smaller errors
- Predictions will be centered around the true value, avoid really large errors


## Why OLS?

Why do we use OLS in this class?

- Simple, linear relationship is a good starting point for modeling
- Mathematical trick makes it "easy" to find $b$ values that minimize MSE
- Predictions from OLS have desirable properties
  - OLS is the best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE)
  - "Best" means most precise
  - "Unbiased" means predictions are correct on average
  
## Other Models

There are many other modeling approaches used in the real world

- Relax or fully abandon the linear functional form
- Trade some bias for improved precision
- Implement alternative loss functions
- Address cases where there are many features to choose between

# Modeling using OLS

## A modeling question

Suppose I am interested in the impact of average temperature on avocado yields

- How might I investigate this relationship?
- What steps might I take to get there using the data we have?


## Pre-modeling Investigation

From last class:
```{r yield-plot-1}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
ggplot(data=avocado_tmp,aes(x=Value_cru,y=Value_fao)) +
  geom_point(aes(color=ISO3)) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    x="Annual Average Temperature (C)",
    y="Yeild (mt/ha)",
    title="Avocado Yeilds by Country",
    color="Country"
  ) +
  scale_color_viridis_d()
```
What seems to be the biggest driver of yields?


## Modeling a single country

The country seems to matter a lot for yeilds

- We'll think about how to model country effects later
- Let's start off focusing on only Mexico
```{r filter-mexico}
#| echo: true
avocado_tmp |>
  filter(ISO3 == "MEX") -> avocado_tmp_mex
```


## Pre-modeling Investigation

```{r yield-plot-2}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
ggplot(data=avocado_tmp_mex,aes(x=Value_cru,y=Value_fao)) +
  geom_point(color="black",size=3) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    x="Annual Average Temperature (C)",
    y="Yeild (mt/ha)",
    title="Avocado Yeilds in Mexico"
  )
```
Does it seem like there is a relationship between temperature and yields?

## Proposing a model

From our visual analysis

- There may be a relationship between temperature and yields
- If it were linear, we could model it as

$$Yield = b_0 + b_1 Temperature + \epsilon$$

- How do we do this in R?

## Training OLS Models in R

Train OLS models in R using `lm(<formula>,<data>)`

- `<formula>` is an [R Formula](https://www.econometrics.blog/post/the-r-formula-cheatsheet/)
  - Describes the relationship we will model
  - General form `<depvar> ~ <expr>`
- `<data>` is the data frame to use for training
- Returns a trained model object

## Training an OLS Model

Train the following OLS model on the Mexico Avocado Yield data
$$Yield = b_0 + b_1 Temperature + \epsilon$$


## Training an OLS Model - Example

```{r train-ols}
#| echo: true
lm(
  Value_cru ~ Value_fao,
  data=avocado_tmp_mex
) -> yield_model

print(yield_model)
```
